question.text: The race page reports roughly twenty-fold growth in physical qubits from 2019 to 2023 — 1,180 (Atom Computing, 2023) against 53 (Google Sycamore, 2019). Is this a census of every quantum computer built in that window?
options: No — it's the largest announced milestone each year on a hand-curated list; one unlisted machine, or a different counting convention, moves it
Yes — every publicly announced quantum processor from 2019 to 2023 is included in this comparison
No — the comparison is invalid because Atom Computing and Google use completely unrelated qubit technologies
Yes, and the twenty-fold figure is a hard lower bound that any future accounting would only increase
question.hint: What does it take to build a timeline like this — every machine ever announced, or the biggest one anyone reported each year?

explain.g: The chart tracks the largest chip anyone announced in a given year, which is a reasonable way to show a trend but not the same as counting every machine that existed. It also compares "physical qubits" across two very different kinds of hardware — trapped-ion sites and superconducting qubits — where the same word doesn't always mean the same amount of usable hardware.
explain.y: 1,180 ÷ 53 = 22.3×, rounded to roughly twenty-fold. Atom Computing's 1,180 are trap sites in a neutral-atom array, not qubits proven good enough to compute with, and Sycamore's 53 are wired superconducting qubits — two different notions of "physical qubit" sitting on either end of the ratio. A milestone list is also, by construction, incomplete: it tracks what got announced, not a census.
explain.r: tools/verify_hardware.py pulls both milestones from data/hardware.json's curated timeline. "Physical qubits" spans fabricated sites, individually controlled qubits, and qubits good enough to run a real computation with — the three numbers are not interchangeable, and this receipt's own value mixes the first and second across the two years compared.
